title: Spaghetti Cacio e Pepe
subtitle: Roman pecorino and black pepper pasta
excerpt: Spaghetti cacio e pepe is a Roman pasta of three ingredients: spaghetti, pecorino Romano, and black pepper. The technique is simple but unforgiving: the cheese must melt into the starchy pasta water without clumping. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Cacio e pepe is one of the four traditional Roman pasta sauces, alongside carbonara, gricia, and amatriciana. The name means simply cheese and pepper. It is a dish of the Roman campagna tradition, where shepherds travelling with their flocks carried cured pecorino and dried pasta. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), documents pasta dressed with cheese and pepper as a basic Roman preparation. The critical technique, emulsifying the cheese with pasta cooking water to form a sauce, is the one variable that separates a glossy coating from a clumped, grainy one.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hard, aged sheep's milk cheese from the Lazio region around Rome, sharper and saltier than Parmesan. Essential to authentic cacio e pepe: Parmesan alone gives a different result.
The salted water in which pasta has cooked. It becomes thick with dissolved starch and acts as an emulsifier that binds cheese into a sauce without clumping.

content.text: Spaghetti cacio e pepe has three ingredients and one technique that matters: keeping the cheese fluid. Grated

goes into the hot pan off the heat, loosened with ladles of starchy pasta water. The starch in that water is what stops the cheese from seizing into clumps. Get the ratio right and the sauce coats every strand in a glossy, spicy layer.

Use only pecorino Romano, not Parmesan. Parmesan is less salty and melts differently; mixing half and half is a popular variation but not the classic dish. Freshly cracked black pepper is not optional: pre-ground pepper lacks the aromatic heat the dish depends on.

items.prepNote: finely grated, plus extra to serve

content.text: A large pan for the pasta and a wide frying pan, at least 30 cm, for finishing the sauce. Reserve a large jug for the
Toast the pepper and cook the pasta

Crack the black pepper coarsely: use a pestle and mortar or the side of a knife, not a fine grinder. Toast {{black-pepper}} of cracked pepper in the dry wide frying pan over a medium heat for about 1 minute until fragrant. Set aside.

Bring a large pan of water to the boil. Salt it lightly (less salt than usual, since the pecorino is already very salty). Cook {{pasta-dried}} of spaghetti for 1 minute less than the packet says, so it is just short of done. Before draining, scoop out at least 400 ml of the cooking water.

Put the frying pan with the toasted pepper back over a medium heat. Add 150 ml of the pasta cooking water and let it bubble for 30 seconds. Add the drained pasta and toss to coat, adding splashes of cooking water to keep it loose.

Take the pan off the heat. Wait 30 seconds for it to cool slightly, then add {{pecorino-romano}} of grated pecorino in two additions, tossing and adding small splashes of cooking water between each. The cheese must melt into the water to form a sauce, not seize. Work quickly.
Once the sauce is glossy and clings to the pasta, serve immediately. Add more cracked pepper and a little extra pecorino at the table.

items.symptom: Cheese clumps into a rubbery mass
items.cause: Pan was too hot when cheese was added
items.fix: Always take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 30 seconds before adding cheese. The starchy pasta water must be cool enough to emulsify, not hot enough to cook the cheese solid.

items.symptom: Sauce is too thick and sticky
items.fix: Keep adding small splashes of reserved cooking water and toss vigorously. The sauce loosens with each addition.

items.symptom: Sauce is watery and does not coat the pasta
items.cause: Too much pasta water added at once
items.fix: Add water in small amounts, tossing between additions. Let the sauce reduce slightly between splashes.

items.cause: Pepper not toasted, or pre-ground pepper used
items.fix: Toast whole cracked peppercorns in a dry pan until fragrant before using. The toasting opens the aromatic compounds.

content.text: Cacio e pepe is a Roman dish and Romans are proprietary about it. The restaurant versions in the Testaccio and Trastevere neighbourhoods set the standard: a glossy, amber-coloured sauce, aggressive with pepper, rich with cheese. Outside Rome the dish is sometimes made with Parmesan alone or with cream, both of which change its character. The Roman original has no fat beyond what is naturally in the pecorino. Its economy is its logic: the dish exists because shepherds carried cheese, pasta, and pepper. Everything else would have been extra weight.
